items.title: Using AI for just 10 minutes erodes your ability to persist at hard things
items.excerpt: Across three randomized trials with 1,222 participants (UC Berkeley, presented at COLM), people who used an AI helper for ~10 minutes became less persistent and less accurate on fraction and SAT reading problems once it was removed, often giving up, while never-assisted participants did better by the end.
items.rationale: Three randomized trials with 1,222 people found that about 10 minutes of AI help left participants less persistent and less accurate once the help was removed. It is the freshest and most broadly relevant cognitive-science result in the pool.

items.title: Now in Nature: Retrofitting language models to operate over bytes
items.excerpt: The 'byteification' technique behind Ai2's open byte-level Bolmo models, published in Nature with LMU Munich, Cambridge, UW and Imperial, converts existing tokenized LLMs to letter-by-letter models with under 1% of usual training, preserving performance and fixing character-level tasks like spelling backward.
items.rationale: A peer-reviewed Nature paper showing that existing tokenized LLMs can be converted to byte-level models with under 1% of the usual training. The method is open and fixes character-level failures.

items.title: Pollen study reveals the hidden history of grasses
items.excerpt: University of Illinois researchers (PNAS, 'Deep learning of fossil pollen morphology') combine super-resolution microscopy with convolutional neural networks to tell grass pollen apart, estimating species diversity and C3/C4 grasses across a 25,000-year Mount Kenya lake-sediment record.
items.rationale: A PNAS study in which CNNs tell apart grass pollen that people cannot distinguish by eye, recovering 25,000 years of grassland diversity. It is a concrete research result where AI drives the science, in paleoecology, a field not yet covered.

items.title: Neural network study sheds light on how AI chatbots 'reason' like humans
items.excerpt: Yale computational linguist Tom McCoy and Microsoft/NYU co-authors (arXiv) show LLMs' internal vectors can be swapped for role-and-filler symbolic representations with little behavior change, and targeted edits to them steer outputs, which suggests that symbolic-like structure emerges on its own.
items.rationale: Yale, Microsoft and NYU researchers show that LLM internal vectors can be swapped for symbolic role-filler structures with little change in behavior, and that editing those structures steers the output. This is new evidence on cognitive science's symbolic-versus-connectionist debate.

items.title: Spiking neural network learns to predict what will happen, when, and how likely it is
items.excerpt: University of Tokyo WPI-IRCN researchers (Communications Biology) built a 1,000-neuron recurrent spiking network that uses only local learning rules to learn which event a cue predicts, when it arrives and how likely it is, adapting when probabilities shift, with implications for neuromorphic AI.
items.rationale: A Communications Biology paper in which a 1,000-neuron spiking network learns what will happen, when, and how likely it is, using only local brain-like learning rules. It adds computational neuroscience and is a different study from the 09-22 physical-AI hardware card.
